claim: LocoMouse is a novel system for analyzing limb, head, and tail kinematics of freely walking mice.
source: Here we describe a novel system (LocoMouse) for analyzing limb, head, and tail kinematics of freely walking mice.
evidence: The system is described in the manuscript text and illustrated in Figure 1, showing the apparatus and tracking capabilities.

claim: LocoMouse uses high-speed cameras and machine learning algorithms to automatically detect and track the position of paws, nose, and tail in 3D with high (2.5 ms) temporal resolution.
source: The noninvasive, markerless LocoMouse system (Figure 1) uses high-speed cameras and machine learning algorithms to automatically detect and track the position of paws, nose, and tail in 3D with high (2.5 ms) temporal resolution.
evidence: The manuscript describes the technical specifications of the system, including temporal resolution derived from 400 fps recording (1/400 = 2.5 ms).

claim: Purkinje cell degeneration (pcd) mice exhibit characteristic impairments in locomotor coordination.
source: Mutant mice with cerebellar circuit defects exhibit characteristic impairments in locomotor coordination
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript showing coordination deficits in pcd mice.

claim: Differences in the forward motion of individual paws in pcd mice are fully accounted for by changes in walking speed and body size.
source: Analysis of visibly ataxic Purkinje cell degeneration (pcd) mice reveals that while differences in the forward motion of individual paws are fully accounted for by changes in walking speed and body size
evidence: This claim is supported by the linear mixed-effects models presented in Figures 2 and 3, showing that stride parameters in pcd mice match predictions based on speed and body size.

claim: 3D trajectories, inter-limb coordination, and whole-body coordination are specifically impaired in pcd mice.
source: more complex 3D trajectories and, especially, inter-limb and whole-body coordination are specifically impaired
evidence: This is demonstrated through data in Figures 3-6 showing altered off-axis paw movements, interlimb phasing, and nose/tail oscillations.

claim: The coordination deficits in pcd are consistent with a failure to predict and compensate for the consequences of movement across the body.
source: Moreover, the coordination deficits in pcd are consistent with a failure to predict and compensate for the consequences of movement across the body.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the passive geometric model of tail and nose movements presented in Figure 5.

claim: The cerebellum is critical for coordinated locomotion.
source: The cerebellum is critical for coordinated locomotion; cerebellar damage leads to characteristic gait ataxia across species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Stride length, cadence, swing velocity, and stance duration vary consistently with walking speed in wildtype mice.
source: Each parameter measured, including stride length, cadence, swing velocity, and stance duration (Figure 2C–F), varied consistently with the walking speed of the mouse.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2 showing systematic relationships between these parameters and speed.

claim: Basic stride parameters in mice can be predicted based solely on walking speed and body weight.
source: This analysis revealed that the value of each stride parameter was readily predicted based solely on walking speed and body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the linear mixed-effects models presented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pcd mice are smaller than control mice.
source: Since pcd mice, like many ataxic animals, are smaller than controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in the data comparing body weights between pcd and control mice.

claim: Pcd mice walk more slowly than control mice.
source: and given that they walk more slowly (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the histogram of walking speeds in Figure 3A.

claim: The instantaneous forward paw velocity profiles of pcd mice are not distinguishable from those of size-matched controls across speeds.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the instantaneous forward paw velocity profiles of pcd mice were not distinguishable from those of size-matched controls, across speeds (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E comparing velocity profiles between pcd and size-matched controls.

claim: Pcd mice exhibit a wider base of support than size-matched control mice.
source: Consistent with previous findings of ataxic mice and humans, pcd mice exhibited a wider base of support than size-matched control mice (Figure 3F) (F(15.51,1)=42.87, p <0 0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3F and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Pcd mice show significantly larger vertical displacement of both front and hind paws across speeds.
source: Further, analysis of the vertical (z) trajectories revealed significantly larger vertical displacement of both front and hind paws of pcd mice, across speeds (F(66.84,1)=17.16, p <0 0.001) (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H with statistical support.

claim: Wildtype mice walk in a symmetrical trot pattern across speeds.
source: In our experiments, wildtype mice walked in a symmetrical trot pattern across speeds—each diagonal pair of limbs moved together and alternated with the other pair (Figure 4A, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polar plots and support patterns in Figure 4.

claim: The normal pattern of interlimb coordination is markedly disrupted in pcd due to specific changes in the phase relationship between front and hind limbs.
source: The normal pattern of interlimb coordination was markedly disrupted in pcd, due to specific and consistent changes in the phase relationship between front and hind limbs (F(77.07,1) = 4.11, p <0 0.05; Figure 4A, right; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and 4B with statistical support.

claim: Left-right alternation is maintained in pcd mice.
source: Importantly, in marked contrast to the front-hind limb coupling, left-right alternation was maintained in pcd (F(159,1) = 0.018, p=0.89; Figure 4A, right: red vs blue and cyan vs magenta; Figure 4B, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase analysis in Figure 4 with statistical support.

claim: Pcd mice spend more time with more paws on the ground.
source: Pcd mice spent more time with more paws on the ground (Figure 4D, right; Figure 4E, left) (3-paw support F(82,1) = 83.57, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is shown in the support pattern analysis in Figure 4D and 4E with statistical support.

claim: The walking speed of pcd mice is limited by the need to have at least one hind paw on the ground for postural stability.
source: In other words, it appears that the walking speed of pcd mice is limited by the need to have at least one hind paw on the ground, for postural stability (Stolze et al., 2002).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the observation that pcd walking speeds coincide with the transition from positive to negative % double hind limb supports, as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Pcd mice show an increase in unstable support configurations such as non-diagonal 2-paw support.
source: Despite their slower walking speeds and increased percent of time spent with more paws on the ground, pcd mice also showed an increase in unstable support configurations such as non-diagonal 2-paw support (Figure 4E, right; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (F(46.78,1) = 7.76, p = 0.01)
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4E with statistical support.

claim: The distance between hind paw placement and previous forepaw position is more variable in pcd mice.
source: While the average distance between hind paw placement and previous forepaw position was the same in pcd and controls (F(14,1) = 0.44, p = 0.52), it was more variable in pcd (F(168,1) = 75.30, p < 0.001; Figure 4G), across speeds.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G with statistical support.

claim: Both the nose and tail of pcd mice exhibit large side-to-side oscillations during the locomotor cycle.
source: In control mice, lateral movements of the nose and tail were small (Figure 5A,B, black). In striking contrast, however, both the nose and the tail of pcd mice exhibited large side-to-side oscillations during the locomotor cycle (Figure 5A,B, purple; Video 2) (compared to size-matched controls: nose F(13.48,1) = 5.49, p < 0.05, tail F(415,1) = 91.01, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A and 5B with statistical support.

claim: In pcd mice, both nose and tail become increasingly phase-lagged at faster speeds.
source: However, in pcd both nose and tail (Figure 5E) became increasingly phase-lagged at faster speeds (tail: F(401.02,1) = 5.55,p <0 0.05; nose: F(53.61,1) = 4.89,p <0 0.05 for speeds above 0.1 m/s).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with statistical support.

claim: Tail movements in pcd can be modeled as passive consequences of the forward movement of the hind limbs.
source: The large, sinusoidal amplitude of the tail oscillations and their time-delayed relationship to hind paw movement suggested to us that tail movements in pcd could reflect passive consequences of the forward movement of the hind limbs.
evidence: This hypothesis is tested with a geometric model presented in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claim: The side-to-side tail movements predicted by the passive model are strikingly similar to the tail oscillations of pcd mice.
source: The side-to-side tail movements predicted by the passive model were strikingly similar to the tail oscillations of pcd mice (compare grey dashed lines with purple traces in Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison between model predictions and actual data in Figure 5.

claim: The tail oscillations of pcd mice are fit very well with a passive model that incorporates a 31 ms time delay for the base of the tail plus a fixed delay per additional tail segment.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, the tail oscillations of pcd mice were fit very well, across walking speeds and tail segments, with a passive model that incorporated a 31 ms time delay for the base of the tail (reflecting the initial inertia of the mouse's rear) plus a fixed delay per additional tail segment (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5F showing the model fit to the data.

claim: Nose movements in pcd are consistent with a time-delayed (96 ms) side-to-side movement.
source: A similar model for the nose (Figure 5) was also consistent with a time-delayed (96 ms) side-to-side nose movement in pcd.
evidence: This is shown in the model presented in Figure 5.

claim: In pcd, the tail and nose appear to move as a passive consequence of forward limb motion.
source: Thus, in pcd, the tail and nose appear to move as a passive consequence of forward limb motion.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the successful modeling of nose and tail movements as passive consequences of hindlimb motion.

claim: Tail and nose movements must be actively canceled in wildtype mice to keep the body axis aligned for forward movement.
source: Further, our results suggest that this movement must be actively canceled in wildtype mice to keep the body axis aligned for forward movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that wildtype mice do not show the oscillations predicted by the passive model, while pcd mice do.

claim: In control mice, the movement of different parts of the body is synchronized.
source: During locomotion in control mice, the movement of different parts of the body is synchronized, and vertical nose and tail movements are relatively small (Figure 6A, left).
evidence: This is shown in the ribbon plots in Figure 6A.

claim: In pcd, spatial and temporal coordination across the body is dramatically impaired.
source: In pcd, however, spatial and temporal coordination across the body is dramatically impaired (Figure 6A, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A showing desynchronized movements across body parts.

claim: In control mice, the movement of most body parts is either strongly correlated or anti-correlated.
source: Finally, a correlation analysis reveals that in control mice, the movement of most body parts is either strongly correlated or anti-correlated (i.e. they move either in–or out-of phase with each other; Figure 6B, left, red and blue).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation matrix in Figure 6B.

claim: In pcd mice, the correlations between body part movements are weaker and more variable.
source: In pcd mice, however, the correlations are weaker and more variable (Figure 6B, right).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation matrix in Figure 6B.

claim: The lack of correlational structure in pcd reflects the failure to synchronize the movements of different parts of the body.
source: This lack of correlational structure reflects the failure of pcd mice to synchronize the movements of different parts of the body.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the correlation analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Ataxic pcd mice have specific deficits in coordinating movement in three dimensions across joints, limbs, and body.
source: Taken together, the results of Figures 3–6 suggest that while the forward motion of individual paws is largely spared, ataxic pcd mice have specific deficits in coordinating movement in three dimensions across joints, limbs, and body.
evidence: This conclusion synthesizes the findings from Figures 3-6.

claim: Many existing analyses of mouse locomotion fail to capture the essence of the coordination deficits of ataxic mice.
source: Therefore it has not been clear to what extent exisiting analyses of mouse locomotion capture the essence of the coordination deficits of ataxic mice that are so visible to the human eye (Cendelin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the current study and supported by citations.

claim: Failure to account for differences in walking speed and body size when comparing data across mice can lead to nonspecific effects being misinterpreted as symptoms of ataxia.
source: This important result highlights that failure to account for differences in walking speed and body size when comparing data across mice and strides can lead to nonspecific effects being misinterpreted as symptoms of ataxia (Koopmans et al., 2007; Cendelin et al., 2010; Wuehr et al., 2012; Batka et al., 2014).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the finding that stride parameters in pcd are normal when accounting for speed and body size, and is supported by citations.

claim: Left-right alternation during locomotion is generated within the spinal cord itself.
source: Interestingly, while front-hind paw coupling was dramatically altered in pcd, left-right alternation was preserved entirely, consistent with the idea that such alternation is generated within the spinal cord itself (Crone et al., 2009; Kiehn, 2011; Dougherty et al., 2013).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the preservation of left-right alternation in pcd and is supported by citations.

claim: The major neuroanatomical finding in pcd is the complete postnatal degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and subsequent loss of granule cells and related structures.
source: The major neuroanatomical finding in pcd is the complete postnatal degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and subsequent loss of granule cells and related structures (Mullen et al., 1976; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Morton and Bastian, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The preservation of forward paw motion in pcd likely reflects the presence of compensatory mechanisms resulting from the chronic loss of Purkinje cells.
source: The most likely interpretation of the surprisingly intact forward paw motion in pcd is that it reflects the presence of inevitable compensatory mechanisms resulting from the chronic loss of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cerebellum provides internal models for motor control.
source: While many lines of evidence suggest that the cerebellum provides internal models for motor control (Wolpert et al., 1998; Ito, 2008), there has been disagreement about the nature of these models (Ebner and Pasalar, 2008; Medina, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The cerebellum may act as an inverse model that computes a command to achieve desired movement.
source: Studies from some systems, including eye movements, have suggested that the cerebellum acts as an inverse model that computes a command to achieve desired movement (Shidara et al., 1993).
evidence: This hypothesis is cited from previous literature.

claim: The cerebellum may provide a forward model that predicts the consequences of movements.
source: Other work, particularly on reaching movements, the cerebellar-like nuclei of electric fish, and locomotor adaptation, has suggested that the cerebellum provides a forward model that predicts the consequences of movements (Bastian et al., 1996; Kennedy et al., 2014) (Pasalar et al., 2006) (Morton and Bastian, 2006).
evidence: This hypothesis is cited from previous literature.

claim: The absence of forward models could form the basis for impaired coordination associated with gait ataxia in mice.
source: Therefore our results raise the intriguing possibility that the absence of forward models, rather than a failure to execute appropriate movement kinematics per se, could form the basis for impaired coordination associated with gait ataxia in mice.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claim: The specific features of gait ataxia vary across mouse models.
source: Although cerebellar involvement is a shared feature across ataxic mouse mutants, the details of the motor phenotypes are different for different mutations (Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous literature.

claim: Patients with cerebellar damage exhibit varying degrees and features of ataxia.
source: Similarly, patients with cerebellar damage exhibit varying degrees and features of ataxia (Morton and Bastian, 2003, 2007; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous literature.

claim: A single high-speed camera captured side and bottom views at 400 fps in the LocoMouse apparatus.
source: A single high-speed camera captures side and bottom views at 400 fps.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The LocoMouse corridor is 66.5 cm long and 4.5 cm wide.
source: Mice walked across a glass corridor, 66.5 cm long and 4.5 cm wide (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A mirror was placed at 45 deg under the mouse to allow simultaneous recording of bottom and side views.
source: A mirror was placed at 45 deg under the mouse, so that a single high-speed camera (AVT Bonito, 1440x250 pixels @400 frames per second) recorded both bottom and side views.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Data collection was automatically triggered by infrared sensors that detected when the mouse entered and exited the corridor.
source: Data collection was performed in LABVIEW and was automatically triggered by infrared sensors that detected when the mouse entered and exited the corridor.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Machine learning algorithms identify paws, nose and tail segments and track their movements in 3D.
source: Machine learning algorithms identify paws, nose and tail segments and track their movements in 3D.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Individual strides were divided into swing and stance phases for analysis.
source: The stride cycles of all four paws were automatically divided into swing and stance phases for subsequent analysis (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A total of 34 wild-type C57BL/6 mice were used for the linear mixed-effects model.
source: A total of 34 wild-type C57BL/6 mice were used for the linear mixed-effects model in Figure 2.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The diverse group of wildtype mice included a variety of ages (30–114 days), body lengths (61–100 mm), and weights (7–33g).
source: The diverse group included a variety of ages (30–114 days), body lengths (61–100 mm), and weights (7–33g).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cadence and stride length increase with walking speed in mice.
source: Cadence and stride length increased with walking speed, indicating that faster walking in mice is associated with longer, more frequent strides (Clarke and Still, 1999; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Batka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations.

claim: Swing velocity increases linearly with walking speed.
source: These changes, in turn, resulted from linear increases in swing velocity and steep decreases in stance duration with increasing walking speed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Stance duration decreases steeply with increasing walking speed.
source: These changes, in turn, resulted from linear increases in swing velocity and steep decreases in stance duration with increasing walking speed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Adding age or gender did not improve predictions of stride parameters once body size was taken into account.
source: While basic stride parameters also varied with gender and age, these effects were related to differences in body size (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); adding neither age nor gender improved the predictions once body size was taken into account.
evidence: This is shown in the model comparison in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pcd mice can be easily identified by eye based on their ataxic, uncoordinated movements.
source: Pcd mice can be easily identified by eye based on their ataxic, uncoordinated movements (Mullen et al., 1976; Le Marec and Lalonde, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous literature.

claim: Pcd mice exhibit impaired rotarod performance.
source: Pcd mice exhibit impaired rotarod performance and deficits in eyelid conditioning that have been attributed to their cerebellar abnormalities (Chen et al., 1996; Le Marec and Lalonde, 1997).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The motor deficits of pcd mice are relatively mild compared to other spontaneous ataxic mutants.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, given the severity of their anatomical phenotype, the motor deficits of pcd mice are relatively mild compared to other spontaneous ataxic mutants (Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Le Marec and Lalonde, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous literature.

claim: Pcd mice were visibly ataxic when walking on the LocoMouse setup.
source: Pcd mice were visibly ataxic when walking on the LocoMouse setup (Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Video 2.

claim: Swing length variability was unchanged in pcd compared to size matched controls.
source: Analysis of the coefficient of variation revealed that swing length variability was unchanged in pcd compared to size matched controls (F(81,1)=0.14, p = 0.0.71).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: Both cadence and stance duration were less variable in pcd.
source: Surprisingly, both cadence and stance duration were less variable in pcd (cadence: F(80,1)=6.90, p < 0.05; stance duration: F(80,1)=6.90, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: Peak swing velocities increased with faster walking speeds but did not vary by genotype.
source: Peak swing velocities increased with faster walking speeds but did not vary by genotype (F(10.97,1)=.092, p = 0.77).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: There was no difference in variability of peak swing velocity between genotypes.
source: There was also no difference in variability of peak swing velocity between genotypes (F(81,1)=0.27, p = 0.60).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: Pcd mice exhibited significantly larger vertical displacement of both front and hind paws across speeds.
source: Further, analysis of the vertical (z) trajectories revealed significantly larger vertical displacement of both front and hind paws of pcd mice, across speeds (F(66.84,1)=17.16, p <0 0.001) (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support and shown in figures.

claim: The variability of vertical displacement was not different in pcd.
source: The variability of this vertical displacement was not different in pcd (F(81,1)=2.47, p = 0.12).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: At slower speeds wildtype mice showed a tendency toward a 'walking trot'.
source: According to the terminology of Hildebrand (1989), at slower speeds there was a tendency toward a 'walking trot' (front paws in a diagonal pair touch down just before hind paws and the paws are on the ground more than 50% of the time)
evidence: This is stated with reference to Hildebrand's terminology.

claim: At faster speeds wildtype mice showed a 'running trot'.
source: while at faster speeds a 'running trot' was observed (diagonal paw pairs strike the ground near-simultaneously and paws are on the ground less than 50% of the time) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Hildebrand's terminology and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no abrupt shift between gait patterns—stance phases varied smoothly with walking speed and duty cycle.
source: There was no abrupt shift between these gait patterns—stance phases varied smoothly with walking speed and duty cycle (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (cf. Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Galloping or bounding was not observed even at the highest speeds.
source: We did not observe galloping or bounding even at the highest speeds (cf. Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015), probably because the mice freely initiated trials in our experiments, rather than being placed in the corridor by the experimenter at the start of each trial (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with a proposed explanation.

claim: Front-hind phasing was not more variable in pcd.
source: Further, the changes in interlimb phasing were consistent—front-hind phasing was not more variable in pcd (F(164,1) = 2.88, p = 0.091)
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: Left-right phasing was less variable in pcd.
source: and in fact left-right phasing was even less variable (F(166,1) = 9.70, p = 0.0021).
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: The average distance between hind paw placement and previous forepaw position was the same in pcd and controls.
source: While the average distance between hind paw placement and previous forepaw position was the same in pcd and controls (F(14,1) = 0.44, p = 0.52)
evidence: This is stated with statistical support.

claim: In control mice, both the tail and nose were phase-locked to the stride cycle across walking speeds.
source: In control mice, both the tail and nose were phase-locked to the stride cycle across walking speeds (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The phase relationships for both the nose and the tail in pcd were consistent with their being time-, rather than phase-locked, to the locomotor cycle.
source: Interestingly, the phase relationships for both the nose and the tail in pcd were consistent with their being time-, rather than phase-locked, to the locomotor cycle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tail was modeled as anchored at a right angle to a point that bisected a line connecting the two hind paws.
source: To investigate this possibility, we generated a simple geometrical model of a mouse (Figure 5C; 'Materials and methods') in which the tail was anchored at a right angle to a point that bisected a line connecting the two hind paws.
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: The orthogonal coupling between the line connecting the hind paws and the tail segments caused the modeled tail to oscillate from side-to-side as the hind paws moved forward.
source: As illustrated in Video 3, the orthogonal coupling between the line connecting the hind paws and the tail segments caused the modeled tail to oscillate from side-to-side as the hind paws moved forward.
evidence: This is shown in Video 3.

claim: Hindpaw alternation is unaltered in pcd.
source: Importantly, these oscillations cannot be accounted for by differences in hind limbs between control and pcd, because: (1) hindpaw alternation is unaltered in pcd (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Hindlimb double support is unaltered in pcd.
source: (2) hindlimb double support is unaltered in pcd (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Though the base of support is wider in pcd, the model predicts that this difference alone would result in smaller, not larger tail oscillations in pcd.
source: and (3) though the base of support is wider in pcd, the model predicts that this difference alone would result in smaller, not larger tail oscillations in pcd.
evidence: This is an inference from the geometric model.

claim: LocoMouse presents several advantages when compared to available systems for analyzing mouse locomotion.
source: LocoMouse presents several advantages when compared to available systems for analyzing mouse locomotion (Hamers et al., 2001; Hoogland et al., 2015; Leblond et al., 2003; Kale et al., 2004; Garnier et al., 2008; Zörner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to other systems.

claim: Mice walk freely and naturally across the LocoMouse corridor.
source: Mice walk freely and naturally across the corridor and throughput is maximized via fully automated data collection and analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the system's features.

claim: The high spatiotemporal resolution of LocoMouse provides detailed 3D paw kinematics.
source: The high spatiotemporal resolution provides detailed 3D paw kinematics.
evidence: This is a description of the system's capabilities.

claim: LocoMouse tracks nose and tail movements during locomotion, which have not been previously reported in freely walking mice.
source: LocoMouse also tracks nose and tail movements during locomotion, which have not been previously reported in freely walking mice.
evidence: This is stated as a novel feature of the system.

claim: The automated tracking algorithm does not measure joint angles.
source: While the automated tracking algorithm does not measure joint angles, these can be incorporated either through hand-labeling or potentially with the use of additional markers.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current system.

claim: Assessments of mouse motor coordination phenotypes often rely on indirect measures.
source: Because of the significant challenges associated with quantifying whole-body coordination in freely walking animals, assessments of mouse motor coordination phenotypes often rely on indirect measures (Mullen et al., 1976; Herbin et al., 2007; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Guillot et al., 2008; Brooks and Dunnett, 2009; Cendelin et al., 2010; Stroobants et al., 2012; Sheets et al., 2013; Suidan et al., 2013; Camera et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated with extensive citations.

claim: Indirect measures of motor coordination lack specificity.
source: While these can be sensitive markers for global motor dysfunction, they lack specificity.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of indirect measures.

claim: Performance on coordination tasks does not necessarily correspond to the degree of gait ataxia during overground locomotion.
source: Moreover, performance on coordination tasks, or even on a treadmill (Hamers et al., 2001; Hoogland et al., 2015), does not necessarily correspond to the degree of gait ataxia during overground locomotion (Herbin et al., 2007; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2007; Guillot et al., 2008; Cendelin et al., 2010; Stroobants et al., 2012; Suidan et al., 2013; Camera et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with extensive citations.

claim: The gene affected in pcd mice encodes ATP/GTP binding protein 1.
source: The gene affected encodes ATP/GTP binding protein 1 [Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2002]
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Heterozygous Purkinje cell degeneration mice on a C57BL/6 background were obtained from Jackson labs.
source: Heterozygous Purkinje cell degeneration mice on a C57BL/6 background were obtained from Jackson labs (#0537 B6.BR-Agtpbp1pcd/J).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments were conducted on wildtype controls (n = 9602 strides; N = 34 mice; 23 male; 11 female; 7-33g, 30–114 days old).
source: Experiments were conducted in two groups: (a) wildtype controls (n = 9602; N = 34 mice; 23 male; 11 female; 7-33g, 30–114 days old)
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments were conducted on homozygous pcd mice (n = 3052 strides; N = 3 mice; 2 female, 1 male; 10–16 g; run at several ages each between 41-154 days old).
source: and (b) homozygous pcd mice (n = 3052; N = 3 mice; 2 female, 1 male; 10–16 g; run at several ages each between 41-154 days old)
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Experiments were conducted on pcd littermates (n = 2256 strides; N = 7 mice; 3 female, 4 male; 15–40 g; 34–190 days old).
source: and their littermates (n = 2256; N = 7 mice; 3 female, 4 male; 15–40 g; 34–190 days old).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Size-matched controls for pcd animals (n = 3400 strides; N = 11 mice) were taken from the wildtype data set.
